comments.author: icyfox
comments.textRawHtml:
Some takes (and from talking to nvidia people):

- Delaware precedent in Caremark has a very high bar for culpability of boards in matters like this. So I suspect the combination of DoJ saying they won't prosecute combined with this standard will successfully remove their individual liability.

- I'm surprised this decision was completely unanimous at the board level, considering how they quickly forced him out. Full 180 in under two weeks.

- The news media is really confusing selling chips to Megaspeed then hosting them in Malaysia (giving chinese companies access - afaik still legal under the old export regime) and Megaspeed smuggling these physical chips for hosting in Chinese data centers. Former was legal and second was not.

- I would not be surprised if a pardon was mentioned at some point. Will be watching how state AGs end up getting involved. CA has already subpoenaed Nvidia for this.

- There was a drum circle at Nvidia from employees who were petitioning to get him back

Disclosure: I co-host a podcast that talks about this. More discussion if anyone is interested: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=t8nLiELIhwA

comments.author: djoldman
comments.textRawHtml:
These proofs really are quite huge. The proof is 1.3GB, ~15M lines of code:

  mkdir -p riemann_proof && cd riemann_proof

  # fetch parts 01–14
  for i in {01..14}; do
    curl -fSL -o lean.tar.gz.part$i https://alpo.ge/lean.tar.gz.part$i || { echo "failed: part$i"; break; }
  done

  # join and decompress (creates ./lean)
  cat lean.tar.gz.part{01..14} > lean.tar.gz
  tar xzf lean.tar.gz

  # size, file count, line counts
  du -sh lean | cut -f1 | xargs printf '%s on disk (lean folder)\n'
  find lean -name '*.lean' | wc -l | xargs printf '%s .lean files\n'
  find lean -name '*.lean' -print0 | xargs -0 cat | wc -l | xargs printf '%s lines total\n'
  find lean -name '*.lean' -print0 | xargs -0 cat | grep -cv '^[[:space:]]*$' | xargs printf '%s non-blank lines\n'

All 175,187 modules seem to check out with Lean 4.33.1, with no errors or `sorry`. There are tons of linter warnings - over 460k of them - but I think they might be caused by the way I invoked it. I haven't checked the actual axiom being proved, though - I'm not good at math :)

children.author: fspeech
children.textRawHtml: It is probably not that compressible. Anthropic FLT proof also has a lot of redundancies but my projection is without true mathematical refactoring it will be hard to get to 50% reduction in line count. One problem is that Lean, or type theory really, is truly verbose. In these parallely developed proofs if two agents use slightly incompatible definitions there are a lot of translations back and forth. Also FLT is following routes well established by mathematicians and it still got to 13 million lines. So I am actually surprised that GRH is not much bigger, as it reportedly ranges over a wide swath of fields.

children.author: nilkn
children.textRawHtml:
I've been thinking about what I'd do if I were in this situation.

Keep it tight and have a few trusted mathematicians review? You're at the risk of Anthropic throwing millions of dollars and internal models at it and beating you, which is exactly what Levent just did.

Try to formalize it yourself? You can't, because that would cost millions of dollars at this scale. Your university system can't afford that, and if you give a lab even a hint of how you did it they'll scoop you immediately.

Just dump it out in public, knowing it's not fully reviewed, hasn't been formalized, and could contain a fatal mistake? Anyone sharing an unverified proof of something as legendary as Riemann, spread over nearly 1,000 pages, would not necessarily be taken seriously, especially after the ABC fiasco. People have been doing this for 100+ years. You'd also just be giving fuel to the labs to build on and potentially take credit away from you if you did actually nearly have a solution.

What was the winning strategy? Or was there none? Perhaps letting a lab burn massive compute on a formal solution, then releasing your attempt same day, really was the optimal strategy.

children.author: palata
children.textRawHtml:
> An interesting strategy

Is it, though?

As a developer, before AI, I took pride in solving challenging problems. I could show them and say: "this was hard, but I persisted and I solved it". Not that they would change the world, but it was obvious that they were challenging.

AI completely changed that: even if I now solved such a problem "manually", people will just assume that it wasn't that hard now that we have AI. Do I want to be the guy who really insists on saying that "no, no, I promise, I solved it on my own"? Then others will just think "yeah you wasted time, you could have used AI".

I believe it may be the same for Masullo: he worked on that for 12 years. If now he partners with an AI company, people will just think "sure, he failed at it for 12 years, and now AI solved it for him". I think he's screwed anyway: even if his current proof is correct (or almost correct), people can assume he quickly finished it with AI. I have never worked on a challenging problem for 12 years, I can only imagine how hard it would be to have it destroyed by AI.

I don't think anyone can "discover" anything today and get the same kind of credit they would have 5 years ago. AI broke that, period.

Do I want to be the guy who really insists on saying that "no, no, I promise, I solved it on my own"? Then others will just think "yeah you wasted time, you could have used AI".

I believe it may be the same for Masullo: he worked on that for 12 years. If now he partners with an AI company, people will just think "sure, he failed at it for 12 years, and now AI solved it for him". I think he's screwed anyway: even if his current proof is correct (or almost correct), people can assume he quickly finished it with AI. I have never worked on a challenging problem for 12 years, I can only imagine how hard it would be to have it destroyed by AI.

I don't think anyone can "discover" anything today and get the same kind of credit they would have 5 years ago. AI broke that, period.

children.author: jychang
children.textRawHtml:
Correct.

They don't use some random definition of RiemannHypothesis, they use the version here: https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib...

Note that this definition is years old. It's very well vetted. It's not a case of "the proof works, it just doesn't actually prove what you think it proves".

If you read the blog post, it says they added a "Challenge.lean" file. What that means is that instead of taking for granted the proof is trying to prove Riemann, they added a small file which reads RiemannHypothesis from the Mathlib library mentioned above, and forces the proof to match that.

They also mention running comparator, which is important because it checks for all the ways a proof might mathematically "cheat". For example, if you are trying to prove 1+2=5, and you redefine 2 as 4, then your bad proof would actually compile in Lean at first, but then comparator checks would discover all the tricks like that and declare the proof invalid.

Additionally, they mention compiling the proof with different Lean kernels, not just the mainline one. This rules out a way a proof This means the proof cannot just take advantage of a bug in the mainline Lean kernel. Importantly, they mention compiling the proof with con-leche, which uses a kernel that has been mathematically verified. Using con-leche is a lot slower, but the fact that the proof works on multiple kernels including con-leche means that it's not taking advantage of some bug in Lean.

At this point, I would say the proof is almost certainly true. The only obvious way it could be false is if ZFC itself is inconsistent or something wild like that, and the proof took advantage of it. But if ZFC is inconsistent, all of mathematics is in trouble.

children.author: btilly
children.textRawHtml:
Yes, Lean is stronger than ZFC. But two of the checkers, con=leche and con-ron, don't just verify based on Lean. They come with a formal proof from set theory that they cannot wind up accepting an incorrect proof.

In other words you can ignore Lean. We have a proof from ZFC, of the Riemann Hypothesis. We have a proof, acceptable in ZFC, that this proof is correct.

In other words Lean's dependent type theory is used to arrange its understanding of the proof. But the actual reasoning that you wind up with for this proof does not need anything that doesn't follow from ZFC.

I wonder if in N years, when we (might) have crazy ASIs that make Fable 5.2 look like a nematode, maybe we'll see things like this as completely trivial and banal.

A machine intelligence might devise something as (seemingly) difficult as the Riemann hypothesis, but checking if what it posits is correct might be like a fast test command in a git repo, and so it can keep iterating on many ideas without being bottlenecked by waiting centuries or, perhaps even hours, to know if the ideas are true.

But then one could even imagine they'll one day be so powerful they could do this and more without ever using a formal system. They will just naturally be that comprehensive and rigorous internally, with something like Lean making them 100% instead of 99.99..% confident.

And eventually this would extend to almost everything, besides maybe biology where it may only be able to compress a human century into a day rather than into a second.

Work and learning lose its value when anyone can reproduce it without you, and when they can do it more trivially even than searching for your version. There are no more publishings of the most advanced knowledge and learnings, because everyone is expected to re-derive it from the prerequisites. It's not as natural and effortless as a large language model working through the course of whatever may require the knowledge and deriving it all in a depth first manner.

children.author: mrandish
children.textRawHtml:
> become smart as the AIs

Treating "intelligence" as a single trait that can be cranked up like an RPG stat bar is a category error built on an ill-defined term.

"Intelligence" is a broad umbrella label for a variety of different capabilities: working memory, pattern matching, sensory integration, long-term recall, and domain-specific knowledge. LLMs running on designed digital silicon are fundamentally different from human minds running on evolved analog biology. They operate on separate substrates with divergent architectures, trade-offs, constraints and failure modes.

LLMs are fantastically useful tools that already beat humans at specific tasks. We built them to simulate specific human intellectual output we find valuable, but they do so using mechanisms which have almost nothing in common with how a brain works. Scaling up the simulation to increase the number and depth of tasks doesn't mean the underlying process is on a path to fully replace human cognition and reasoning.

children.author: mcherm
children.textRawHtml:
I am not certain which "last time" you are thinking of, but I suspect that the answer IS the Lean verification.

If an AI writes a paper with an argument that X is true, it might be that X is true, or it might be that the argument in the paper is subtly flawed and X isn't true

On the other hand, if an AI generates a step-by-step proof in which each step can be mechanically verified, then people might have problems understanding the underlying ideas, but once it has been verified we know it won't have subtle errors. And that is basically what Lean is.

In this case, they not only have a Lean proof, they've verified it with more than one verification tool (so it's unlikely to be a bug in the verification tool) and double-checked whether the thing being proved really is what we intended to prove. That's rock solid.

Getting an UNDERSTANDING of the proof is another challenge, but at this point we can be quite certain it doesn't have errors.

children.author: lelanthran
children.textRawHtml:
> Ford and GM have been doing this since 2002 with the GM–Ford 6-speed automatic transmission [0]

All the manufacturers have been doing it since even before that, with major items like engines and transmissions.

What they haven't been doing is standardising all those other parts that need replacing. For example, standardising on the wheel hub+knuckle for 15-inch, 16-inch, 17-inch and 18-inch wheels will let wheels of the specific size use the same disks, calipers, pads, balljoint, wheel bearing, CV joint and all the sensors (wheel speed, brake, etc).

I see no reason why two different SUVs on 17-inch wheels need completely different brake pads shapes, when both sets have the same surface area, require the same performance profile, etc, but that's what we have now.

You can do the same with almost every mechanical and electrical subsystem in a car, and still have a large variety in cars produced. After all, car manufacturers don't manufacture their own tyres and batteries, do they? They don't manufacture they own wheels.

Even the things that are specific to them, they outsource anyway - they don't each have their own windscreen manufacturer, they outsource that. The already outsource all the glass, all the oils and fluids, all the pipes, etc, it's jus that they produce incompatible designs so that the actual parts manufacturer has to charge a jig setup fee for each of them. Standardising on parts brings in economies of scale.

We need right to repair (for many many good reasons), but this must be reframed and articulated to legacy car manufacturers as Commoditize your complement.

As a mechanical engineer this comment strikes me as too optimistic and borderline naive.

There are hundreds of reasons why different steering components have different shapes. By the time you are down to designing the steering knuckles and wheel hubs of cars, you are already working with vehicle weight, geometry constraints (which are a big deal), backward compatibility to simplify supply chain, material availability, outside suppliers, manufacturability, steering ratios, existing tooling, trying to minimize unsprung weight, servicability, whether the car uses a mcpherson strut or some other suspension setup, FWD vs AWD, etc, etc, etc.

It is almost an overconstrained problem to design these parts for a single vehicle. The combinatorial explosion of how many different ways there are to design the part is worse than you think it is.

Brakes got big and dirverse because "muh handlig" and "muh moose test" (and "muh $500 replacement rim when you hit a curb) drive tire and rim size. Big rims add weight. So they make the brakes lighter by using a bigger diameter rotor and smaller/lighter caliper. The move from traditional spindles and/or press in bearings to bolt on unit bearings hasn't helped either since you're carrying around a few pounds of extra mounting flange.

A big honking cast iron caliper grabbing 12" rotor that mounts from the back of the hub (to reduce the hat diameter letting you have swept area right up to the wheel bolt circle) can really take some heat and the whole thing will package in a 16" rim. But it ain't gonna be light. I get that we're gonna have different "classes" of performance and you won't put that brake assembly on a new land rover even if it has comparable demands to the old van but there is a whole lot of room to consolidate here.

These are still people with personal ambitions beyond a mere paycheck; those wanting easy guaranteed money would simply invest more. Not run a business.

You can do it for 'free' or a nominal charge. This is an easy way to network with successful former executives who still have contacts in the industry.

comments.author: nik_s
comments.textRawHtml:
I think the layman's perception of the increase in survival (~13 months versus ~6 months) will make this look underwhelming. Nevertheless, it's important to remember that the incentives for clinical trials is to only include very late-stage patients who have exhausted all other options (faster trials, smaller sample sizes, surrogate endpoints, a shot at accelerated approval, ...). The fact that a treatment shows promise for these patients that are often in very poor health and considered "hopeless" by today's medicine is exceedingly rare, and the signal from this trial is indeed strong.

The (somewhat reasonable) hope is that patients 1. with earlier forms of pancreatic cancer (non-metastatic) 2. that can undergo surgery 3. together with a (neo)adjuvant treatment with these kras inhibitors, will end up having a much lower recurrence rate and a chance for a long, healthy life.

I think this is genuinely good news worth celebrating!

children.author: boplicity
children.textRawHtml:
This is how most the world operates: people work hard to feed their families and provide security for them. It can be stressful. Money, of course, isn't earned for the sake of money, at least not for most people. That's the claim in the original quote that is completely wrong. Rather, we need money in order to buy food and all of the things that make life decent.

Also, what the quote gets totally wrong: Wealth is strongly correlated with good health. People generally earn more money and become more healthy. Not the other way around, in general, at least.

This is also how the world works: You're quietly eating on a field, when suddenly, you're a meal for an eagle, or a coyote, or a fox. It's short, painful, and brutal. Far better to deal with money, in my opinion, than the harsh reality of the natural world.

children.author: hinkley
children.textRawHtml:
The thing with Buddhism is the notion that many of our injuries are self inflicted or even conjured out of nowhere, and you just exhibited a top shelf example of that.

What I quoted has absolutely nothing to do with karma, and everything to do with how scared you are of dying with regrets. I understand the people who want to see their kid graduate. But just in general principle? Fighting for two more months when even more of that time will be in agony than if you did nothing, and spending your kids inheritance to do that? Why do we do that to ourselves? And why do we sign them up to watch? You can sort out your conflicts with your friends and family in a week, or you can’t sort them out at all. Car wrecks and heart attacks take even that away. At least a terminal illness gives you a last call.

Cancer is cruel. Cancer treatment is only less cruel, and still cruel enough that people volunteer to work in cancer wards to make the patients a little more comfortable (my ex signed up for one but couldn’t follow through).

“Time” is not a reason to stay. It’s a placeholder for magic thinking or something you don’t want to face. And when someone asks YOU what you want to have before you die, you’d better have an answer or you’ll waste it. “Time” is the answer you give when you don’t know the answer and you’re hoping you’ll think of it later. By the time you’re fifty you’ll already know that’s bullshit, or you’ll be buried having never suspected.
